messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

It was the water that Kai remembered first, and the smell—a thick, sweet rot of mud and gasoline that coated everything. The tsunami had swept through his coastal village in the early morning, tearing his wife from his grasp as they tried to climb to the roof. He had been an auditor for the local government then, a man who lived by spreadsheets and certainties. In the aftermath, he had clung to a splintered doorframe for hours, listening to the screams fade, tasting the salt and debris on his tongue. Now, forty-six and widowed, he worked in a high-rise office in a Midwestern city, a thousand miles from any ocean, yet he could still smell that mud when he least expected it—sometimes while driving, sometimes while sitting at his desk, the odor so vivid it made him gag. The memory was so extreme, so far beyond anything he had ever known, that some days it felt like a story that had happened to someone else, a film he had watched rather than a life he had lived.

These memories were not random. They came, he had noticed, when he let his guard down. A quiet evening at home, the silence settling around him like a blanket—that was when the taste would rise in his throat. He had learned to dread silence, because it meant something dangerous was about to happen. So he kept the television on, always, even when he was not watching. He smoked constantly, the ritual of lighting a cigarette and inhaling the sharp, familiar burn giving him something to focus on besides the creeping sense of dread. He had stopped going to unfamiliar places because he could not assess the danger; a new grocery store, a friend’s house in a different neighborhood—these felt like traps. Even delays became omens. If the bus was late, he was certain an accident had occurred. If a colleague was slow to respond to an email, he assumed the worst.

He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that bad things happened and he could not stop them. He felt dead inside, hollowed out, and this numbness was a kind of protection. He avoided relaxing because relaxation felt like surrender, a lowering of defenses that would invite disaster. He did not talk about the tsunami with anyone; even a casual question about his past made his chest tighten, so he changed the subject or excused himself. He had become certain that if he allowed himself to feel happy or relaxed, the other shoe would drop. That feeling of happiness had become a trigger in itself, a flicker of warmth that immediately sent a spike of cold fear through him—because joy had been the last thing he felt before the wave came. He remembered that morning, waking up beside his wife, the sun streaming in, and how that perfect peace had been shattered. So now, when he felt a moment of ease, he would reach for his cigarettes, or find a reason to be busy, or simply sit in the dark of his apartment, waiting for the feeling to pass.

The cycle tightened over months. His avoidance reinforced his belief that the world was unsafe; every time he stayed home, every time he refused a social invitation, he proved to himself that he was right to be afraid. The triggers—the silence, the happiness, the unfamiliar street—pulled him back to the memory, and the memory sharpened his sense of threat, which in turn made the triggers more potent. He began to see danger in the ordinary: a door that was slightly ajar, a distant siren, the way the light fell across his living room floor at dusk. He had stopped going to the office gym because the smell of chlorine reminded him of the sea. His colleagues had noticed his withdrawal, his reluctance to travel for work, his flat affect. He had been passed over for a promotion. He did not care.

What finally brought him to seek help was a night in late autumn. He had woken in the dark, disoriented, certain he could hear water rushing. He had stood in his bedroom, drenched in sweat, unable to move. The silence that followed was worse than any sound. He had stood there for a long time, tasting the mud, feeling the doorframe under his fingers, and he had realized he could not keep living this way. He was afraid of what he might do if he did not get help. He was afraid, too, of what the help might require—of talking, of letting go, of feeling something other than dead. But he made the call anyway, his hand shaking as he dialed, because the alternative, he knew, was to drown again.
